# Percentage Formulas Explained: Of, Is-What-Percent, Change

URL: https://math.streamerosai.com/guides/percentage-formulas/

## Percentage formulas explained: of, is-what-percent and percent change

"Percent" means per hundred, so 15% is 15 out of every 100, or 0.15. Almost every percentage question is one of the five below. The percentage calculator does each of them with your own numbers.

### The five formulas

X% of Y = X / 100 x Y 15% of 80 = 12
X is what % of Y = X / Y x 100 12 of 80 = 15%
X is Y% of what = X / (Y / 100) 12 is 15% -> 80
percent change = (new - old) / old x 100 40 -> 50 = +25%
new after Y% change = old x (1 +/- Y / 100) 80 +25% = 100

### Mistake 1: percent versus percentage points

If an interest rate rises from 4% to 5%, it has risen by 1 percentage point. As a percent change it is up 25%, because 1 is a quarter of 4. News stories mix the two, so check which one is meant.

### Mistake 2: a rise and a fall do not cancel

A percentage always applies to the current value. 100 falling by 50% is 50, and 50 rising by 50% is only 75. To get back to 100 from 50 you need a rise of 100%. This is why a share price that halves has to double to recover.

### Mistake 3: adding discounts

Two discounts multiply. 20% off and then 10% off leaves 0.80 x 0.90 = 0.72 of the price, which is 28% off, not 30%. The percentage decrease calculator shows the result for one step at a time.

### Mistake 4: using the wrong base

Percent change is measured against the starting value. From 40 to 50 is +25%, but from 50 to 40 is -20%. If neither value is the starting point, use percent difference, which divides by the average and gives the same answer both ways: 22.22% for 40 and 50. The percent change calculator shows both.

### Mental shortcuts

- 10% of a number: move the decimal point one place left.
- 5%: half of 10%. 1%: move the decimal point two places.
- 15% is 10% plus 5%. 25% is a quarter. 50% is half.

### Worked example: a price with a discount and tax

An item is listed at 1,000. It is on sale at 20% off, and 18% tax is added at the till. The order matters for how you describe it but not for the result of two multiplications: 1,000 x 0.80 = 800 after the discount, then 800 x 1.18 = 944 with tax. Doing it the other way round, 1,000 x 1.18 x 0.80, is also 944, because multiplication can be done in either order. What is not the same is adding the percentages: 1,000 x (1 + 0.18 - 0.20) would be 980, which is wrong.

### Working backwards from a total

A bill is 1,180 and it includes 18% tax. The tax is not 18% of 1,180. The pre-tax price is 1,180 / 1.18 = 1,000, so the tax is 180. Taking 18% of 1,180 gives 212.40, which is the classic wrong answer, because 18% applies to the price before tax, not to the total. The same rule finds the original price before any known percentage change: divide by (1 + the change).

### Percent change in a row

Successive changes multiply. Up 10% and then down 10% is 100 x 1.10 x 0.90 = 99, a net fall of 1%, not zero. Three years of 5% growth is 1.05 x 1.05 x 1.05 = 1.157625, so 15.76% in total, slightly more than 3 x 5% = 15%, because each year&#x27;s growth is on a larger base. The percentage increase calculator does one step; chain the results for several.

### When a percentage is not enough

- A percentage of a very small base looks dramatic: a rise from 2 to 4 cases is up 100%, but 2 more cases. Quote the counts as well.
- Percentages of different groups cannot be added or averaged without weighting them. If 50% of 10 people and 20% of 90 people agree, the combined figure is (5 + 18) / 100 = 23%, not 35%.
- Percent difference and percent change answer different questions. Use change when one value is the starting point and difference when neither is.
All of the formulas on this page are standard arithmetic definitions of percentage and need no external source; each example above can be checked with the calculators linked on this page or with any ordinary calculator.


---

# How to Count Days Between Dates: Inclusive, Exclusive, Working

URL: https://math.streamerosai.com/guides/counting-days-between-dates/

## How to count days between dates: inclusive, exclusive and working days

Asking how many days there are between two dates sounds simple, yet two people can honestly give different answers. The difference is almost always whether the first and last day are counted.

### Exclusive and inclusive counting

The usual calculation subtracts the earlier date from the later one. From 1 January to 31 December 2026 that is 364 days: the start date is day zero and the end date is day 364. Counting both ends gives 365, which is what you want when you ask how many days an event covers. A course that runs Monday to Wednesday covers 3 days, but the difference between the two dates is 2.
Use the days between dates calculator and tick Count the end date too to switch between them.

### Leap years

A year has 366 days if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. So 2024 and 2000 were leap years and 1900 was not. From 1 January 2024 to 1 January 2025 is 366 days.

### Years, months and days

Age and contract periods are quoted in years, months and days. The method is to add whole calendar months to the start date for as long as the result does not pass the end date, then count the days left. Someone born on 15 May 1990 is, on 4 November 2026, 36 years, 5 months and 20 days old: 15 May 1990 plus 36 years and 5 months is 15 October 2026, and 20 days later is 4 November.
When the day does not exist in a month, such as the 31st in a 30-day month, the date moves to the last day of that month. Try it with the age calculator or the date calculator.

### Working days

Working days exclude Saturdays and Sundays. From Monday 2 November to Monday 9 November 2026 there are 7 days but 5 working days. Public holidays differ by country and region, so they are not subtracted; take them off by hand.

### 29 February birthdays

A leap-day birthday has no exact anniversary in three years out of four. Calculators here treat 28 February as the anniversary. Some countries&#x27; laws use 1 March instead, so use the rule that applies where it matters legally.

### Worked example: a seven-week countdown

Wednesday 4 November 2026 to Friday 25 December 2026. Subtracting the dates gives 51 days (26 days left in November after the 4th, plus 25 in December). Counting both ends gives 52. In weeks that is 7 weeks and 2 days, since 7 x 7 = 49. Because the range starts on a Wednesday and ends on a Friday, the working days (Monday to Friday) are 37 if the last day is not counted and 38 if it is. Public holidays inside the range, such as 25 December itself, would come off that number by hand. Adding days works the same way in reverse: 15 March 2026 plus 100 days is 23 June 2026.

### Why computers get this wrong

A common bug is to subtract two timestamps and divide by 24 hours. In a time zone that changes its clocks, a day can be 23 or 25 hours long, so the result is off by a fraction and rounds the wrong way. A calendar-date subtraction, which ignores the time of day, avoids it. The calculators here work on calendar dates, not on timestamps, for that reason.

### Checking a result by hand

- Same year: subtract the day numbers of the year. 4 November is day 308 and 25 December is day 359 of 2026, and 359 - 308 = 51.
- One year later, same date: 365 days, or 366 if 29 February falls between the two dates.
- Weeks: divide by 7 and keep the remainder. 51 / 7 is 7 with 2 left over, so 7 weeks and 2 days.

### Date formats

Numeric dates such as 04/11/2026 mean 4 November in much of the world and 11 April in the United States, which is a frequent source of off-by-months mistakes. The calculators take a date picker value, not typed text, to avoid the ambiguity. For anything written down for others, the unambiguous form is year-month-day (2026-11-04), the format of ISO 8601 and of RFC 3339 ( rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339).
Limits: the working day count skips Saturdays and Sundays only. Some countries have a different working week and every country has its own public holidays, so for payroll, legal or contract deadlines check the rule in the document that governs them.

# About StreamerOS Math Calculators: Free, Private Math

URL: https://math.streamerosai.com/about/

## About

StreamerOS Math Calculators is a small set of free calculators for everyday number questions: percentages and percent change, age, days between dates, adding to a date, hours worked, ratios and averages, with short guides that explain the formulas.
It is built and maintained by Yaseen Khatib, a full-stack AI engineer, as part of the StreamerOS project. Many calculators give an answer without showing how it was reached, so every page here states its formula and works a few examples you can check by hand.

### How the calculators work

Every calculator runs in your browser using standard JavaScript. The numbers and dates you enter, including dates of birth, are processed on your device and are not sent to a server or stored. The site is a static website hosted on GitHub Pages.

### What the results are, and are not

The calculators do exact arithmetic on what you type, and the date logic is tested against known cases. They are general tools, not financial, legal or medical advice. For legal ages and deadlines, check the rules that apply in your country; for example, the date a 29 February birthday is observed differs between countries.

### Who is behind it

The site is run by one person, Yaseen Khatib, a full-stack AI developer based in Hyderabad, India. His portfolio is at yk.streamerosai.com. There is no team and no company behind the pages, which is why corrections go straight to him through the contact page. The same family of small sites also includes tools for developers, money, images and maths at tools, calc, images and math on streamerosai.com.

### How pages are kept accurate

The calculation code has automated tests, every formula is written out on the page with a worked example you can check by hand, and facts that come from outside (rates, rules, standards) name their source. Each page shows the date it was last reviewed, and that date changes only when the page does. The assumptions and limits of a tool are stated on its page rather than hidden, and a result that cannot be right (an impossible date, for instance) shows a message instead of a number. The terms of use and privacy policy describe the rest.

### How the site is funded

The calculators are free. The site does not show ads at the moment; it may show Google AdSense ads to cover hosting and development time. Ads never change the result of a calculator.

### Corrections

If a result is wrong or a guide contains a mistake, please use the contact page. Fixes are made in the open and the guides are updated.

# Privacy Policy: StreamerOS Math Calculators

URL: https://math.streamerosai.com/privacy/

## Privacy Policy

This policy describes what StreamerOS Math Calculators ( https://math.streamerosai.com) does with information when you use it. Last updated: 19 November 2026.

### What the tools do with your input

The calculators work entirely in your browser. The numbers and dates you type, including any date of birth, are not transmitted to our servers, logged, or stored. Closing the page clears them.

### Cookies and similar technologies

Cookies are small files a site stores in your browser. The analytics and advertising services listed below may set cookies or read similar identifiers. The tools themselves do not need a cookie to work. The only thing the site stores for its own use is your light or dark theme choice, kept in your browser&#x27;s local storage and never sent anywhere. You can block or delete cookies in your browser settings; the tools keep working either way.

### Analytics

This site uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits and see which pages are useful. It collects page views, approximate location, device and browser type, and how you arrived, using cookies and similar identifiers. It does not receive the text you enter into the tools. You can opt out with the Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on. We do not sell personal information.

### Usage recording

This site uses Microsoft Clarity to see how pages are used, through heatmaps and anonymised session recordings (mouse movement, clicks and scrolling). Clarity is configured to mask the text on the page, so what you type or load into a tool is not recorded. Clarity sets its own cookies ( _clck, _clsk) and Microsoft cookies on clarity.ms and bing.com (such as MUID); see Microsoft&#x27;s privacy statement.

### First-party visit counter

The site also runs a small counter of its own, Pulse, a script served from our own Cloudflare Worker (pulse.yaseenyk.workers.dev), to tell real visits from automated ones. It records the page address (without the query string), the referring site and campaign tags, country, device type, browser and system name, screen size, language, the name of your network provider, scroll depth, time on the page, page speed, which links and buttons were clicked, and a human-or-bot signal. It sets no cookies, never reads what you type or the values in input fields, and stores no IP address or browser string: the address is used in memory only, to limit abuse and to make a visitor code that changes every day (a one-way hash with a random salt that is deleted the next day), so visits cannot be linked across days. Records are deleted after 90 days. It switches itself off when your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, and on localhost. The data is used only to understand how the site is used.

### Advertising

This site does not show ads at the moment. We intend to use Google AdSense after approval. Once ads run, Google and its partners may use cookies to serve ads based on your visits to this and other websites. You can opt out of personalised advertising at adssettings.google.com, and learn how Google uses data from sites that use its services at policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites. Where required by law (for example in the EEA and UK), personalised ads will be shown only after you consent. Ads will never change a tool&#x27;s result, and this policy will be updated before ads go live if anything above changes.

### Your choices

You can use the site with cookies blocked, opt out of Google Analytics with the add-on above, turn on Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control to switch off the visit counter, and ask a privacy question through the contact page. We do not collect accounts, names or email addresses through the tools. If you write to us, we use your address only to reply.

### Children

The tools are general-purpose and not aimed at children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect their data.

### Contact

Questions about this policy: see the contact page. The rules for using the site are in the terms of use.

The calculators give arithmetic results from the numbers and dates you enter and the method described on each page. Check results that matter. ### Availability and liability

# Contact StreamerOS Math Calculators: Errors and Requests

URL: https://math.streamerosai.com/contact/

## Contact

Found a bug, a wrong result, or want a tool added? Tell us and include the input that caused the problem when you can. Messages go to the person who runs the site, and we aim to reply within a few working days.
Email: contact@streamerosai.com

### What helps most

- The page address and what you expected to see.
- The input that caused a wrong result, with anything private removed, and the browser you used.
- For a mistake in a guide, the sentence and the source you believe says otherwise.

### What we cannot do

We cannot give personal financial, tax, legal or employment advice, check a specific document, or recover a file for you, because nothing you enter is uploaded to us. The site is run by one person, so replies can take a few days. Reports of wrong results are fixed first. If you do not want us to keep your email address, say so and we will delete the message once it is answered.
